study.title: Find the Real Problem
study.question: How do designers find problems worth solving?
study.passage:
Step 1, Observe (10 minutes): In pairs, walk through part of the school (cafeteria, hallways, library, gym, bus line) and note anything that seems frustrating, slow or confusing.
Step 2, Choose a need (5 minutes): Choose one possible need, such as "Students wait too long in the cafeteria line" or "Lost-and-found items never get returned."
Step 3, Research users (20 minutes): Write a 5-question survey and 3 interview questions. Good questions are open and don't lead people.
• Leading: "Don't you hate the slow lunch line?"
• Better: "Describe your experience in the lunch line."
Survey at least 10 students and interview 2.
Step 4, Check assumptions (5 minutes): What did you assume before? Did your research support it or change it?
Step 5, Problem statement (10 minutes): Use the frame: "[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight from research]."
Example: "Grade 7 students need a faster way to get lunch because 7 of 10 surveyed said they have less than 15 minutes to eat after waiting in line."

study.title: Know Your Users
study.question: How do I find out what users really need?
study.passage:
Research brief (written for this lesson): Your team has identified a need: "Students lose track of homework deadlines." Before designing a solution, research the users.
Part 1, Survey (aim for 20 responses from Grades 7–9): Write five questions. Mix closed and open questions. Examples: "How often do you miss a homework deadline? (Never / Sometimes / Often)"; "What do you use now to track homework?"; "What would make tracking homework easier?"
Part 2, Interviews (two people): Ask "Tell me about the last time you missed a deadline. What happened?" Listen more than you talk.
Part 3, Competitor check: Look at two existing solutions (a paper planner, a calendar app). List what users like and dislike about each.
Part 4, Summarize: Count closed-question answers. Group open answers into themes. Write three key findings.

body.hook: "Make an app for homework" is a topic. "Grade 8 students who play sports miss about two deadlines a month because their schedules change weekly" is a problem you can actually solve. A sharp problem statement points straight at a solution.

study.title: Sharpen the Problem
study.question: How do I turn research into a problem I can solve?
study.passage:
Problem-statement formula (written for this lesson):
[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight].
Example from homework research: "Grade 8 students who play team sports need a way to keep track of changing homework deadlines because their practice schedules change each week and they forget to check the class page."
Checklist: Is the user specific? Is the need about the user, not about a product ("an app")? Does the insight come from research? Is the scope small enough for our time?
"How might we" (HMW): Turn the problem into a question: "How might we help student athletes keep track of deadlines when their schedules change?"
Practice: Improve these weak statements: "Students need an app." "Kids are lazy about homework." "Everyone needs to be more organized."
